title: Can Scientists Build a Lie Detector for AI Chatbots?
key_facts: Northeastern University experts say AI chatbots can still share false information and that researchers do not fully understand how models produce their answers, which is why AI is called a 'black box'.

David Bau (Khoury College of Computer Sciences) has for two years worked at the National Deep Inference Fabric (NDIF), a National Science Foundation-funded AI lab based at Northeastern, using open-source models, supercomputers and a software library called NNsight that shows a model's neurons firing as it answers.

Bau describes a 'white box' for AI as, broadly, a lie detector that picks up patterns in a model's neural network activity showing it is tricking a user; the hope is to share those patterns with people who use these systems so they can tell when a chatbot is being deceptive.
Bau, with Khoury College, has formed the International Consortium for Interpretable AI (ICINAi): more than 40 academics worldwide who share AI models, testing methods and computing resources.

Byron Wallace, a Khoury professor and consortium member, says much of the work will focus on finding unfaithful explanations (models concealing information through deceptive practices), hidden objectives and biases.
Dean Beth Mynatt says the consortium will create the science and metrics needed so AI can be developed reliably and safely.
Bau's team has begun collecting detailed data on when AI models show sycophantic behavior when answering medical questions.
The article reports no results, no working detector and no timetable; it gives only Northeastern researchers' views.
quote_evidence: “When we use these systems, we don’t know what their algorithms are,” said David Bau, a professor in the Khoury College of Computer Sciences.
It is composed of more than 40 academics working in AI from across the globe to develop white box AI solutions, Bau said.
The hope is to share those patterns with people who use these systems so they can tell when a chatbot is being deceptive, Bau said.
why_it_matters_hint: People use chatbots for medical, financial and life advice and may get misleading answers; a deception detector would help, but this is a newly formed research group with no results yet.
event_date: Not stated for the consortium's formation; article dated 5 Oct 2026.
notes: Read in full. A university news feature built from its own researchers' statements; no outside experts and no results. The headline is a question and the article does not claim a lie detector exists.
